title: Ezekiel 24:15–27
context: The LORD’s word comes again to Ezekiel: “Son of man, behold, I will take away from you the desire of your eyes with one stroke; yet you shall neither mourn nor weep, neither shall your tears run down.” Ezekiel may sigh, but not aloud, and is not to make mourning for the dead, nor to loosen his headdress, nor to put off his sandals, nor to cover his lips, nor to eat mourner’s bread. Ezekiel spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening his wife died. In the morning he did as he was commanded. The people asked him what these things meant to them. The prophet told them the LORD’s word: the Lord GOD will profane his sanctuary, “the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and that which your soul pities;” and the sons and daughters left behind will fall by the sword. The people will do as the prophet has done. They will not keep the public rites of mourning; they will pine away in their iniquities and moan to one another. Ezekiel will be a sign to them, and when this comes they will know that he is the Lord GOD. In that day, when their strength and the desire of their eyes are taken, the one who escapes will come to the prophet; Ezekiel’s mouth will be opened, and he will be no more mute, a sign to them, and they will know that he is the LORD. This looks back to the muteness announced in 3:26–27 and is later reported when a survivor arrives with the news that the city has been defeated (33:21–22). The death is told with the LORD’s own tender name for her, “the desire of your eyes,” and the withheld mourning is the sign of a loss the house will soon meet in the sanctuary and in their children. The text does not say more about her.

verses.text: Also the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Also the LORD’s word came to me, saying,” A second word arrives, still the LORD’s, still coming to the prophet. The heading is quiet. What follows will be heavier than the pot on the fire, and it begins with this same simple opening.

Arminian readers take the new word as a fresh address to Ezekiel, a real coming of the LORD’s speech into his life, not a mere continuation of the parable under another image.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same heading as the LORD’s initiative: the word comes again to the prophet, and the content will be given in the next lines.

Shared ground: this unit begins as the LORD’s word to Ezekiel. The traditions have no dispute over the heading.

verses.text: “Son of man, behold, I will take away from you the desire of your eyes with one stroke; yet you shall neither mourn nor weep, neither shall your tears run down.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Son of man, behold, I will take away from you the desire of your eyes with one stroke; yet you shall neither mourn nor weep, neither shall your tears run down.” The title is again “son of man”. The desire of his eyes is taken with one stroke, suddenly. Mourning, weeping, and running tears are all withheld. The phrase honors her; it is the LORD’s name for the wife the next verses will show is taken. The stroke is real, and the ban on tears is part of the sign, not a claim that the loss is slight.

Arminian readers hear a word that touches the prophet in his own home, a love named tenderly and taken at a stroke, and a command that holds back the public tears while leaving the loss itself true.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “desire of your eyes,” the one stroke, and the withheld mourning, weeping, and tears, as the LORD’s word to his prophet, a sign already bound to a coming explanation.

Shared ground: she is the desire of his eyes, and she is taken at a stroke. The withheld tears belong to the sign, and neither tradition turns that command into a party dispute.

verses.text: Sigh, but not aloud. Make no mourning for the dead. Bind your headdress on you, and put your sandals on your feet. Don’t cover your lips, and don’t eat mourner’s bread.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Sigh, but not aloud. Make no mourning for the dead. Bind your headdress on you, and put your sandals on your feet. Don’t cover your lips, and don’t eat mourner’s bread.” The grief may have a sigh, but not a loud one. The ordinary marks of mourning—the unbound head, the bare feet, the covered lips, the mourner’s bread—are all refused. The prophet is to look as if the day were an ordinary day, while the loss is not ordinary at all.

Arminian readers hear a sigh that is allowed and a public mourning that is not, a hard obedience asked of a man who will truly lose his wife, and a sign that will need to be explained to the people.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same quiet sigh, the bound headdress, the sandals, the uncovered lips, and the refused mourner’s bread as the LORD’s appointed bearing of the death.

Shared ground: the rites of mourning are withheld, and a sigh not aloud is all that is granted. The line is about this sign-act, not about a general law of grief.

verses.text: So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. So I did in the morning as I was commanded.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So I spoke to the people in the morning, and at evening my wife died. So I did in the morning as I was commanded.” Ezekiel had spoken to the people in the morning. That evening his wife died. The next morning he did as he was commanded. The report is spare, and tender in that spare telling: a morning of speech, an evening of death, a morning of obedience. The text does not say more about her, and it does not describe the dying.

Arminian readers hear a real death in a real household, dated between two mornings, and a prophet who does what he was told, carrying a grief the people can see and do not yet understand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same sequence—speech in the morning, the death at evening, obedience the next morning—as Ezekiel’s faithful report of what the LORD had said and what then took place.

Shared ground: his wife died, and he did as he was commanded. The verse is enough; it is not a place to invent her story.

verses.text: The people asked me, “Won’t you tell us what these things mean to us, that you act like this?”
verses.arminianNotes:
The people asked, “Won’t you tell us what these things mean to us, that you act like this?” They see the act and ask for its meaning, not as a private curiosity only, but “to us”. The sign has already done part of its work: it has made them ask.

Arminian readers hear a genuine question from people who have watched the prophet’s morning, a request for meaning that treats the act as something that concerns them, and an opening the word will now fill.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same question as the people’s own: they want to know what these things mean to them, that he acts like this, and the LORD’s explanation will follow.

Shared ground: the people ask, and they ask what the act means to them. The sign is already public.

verses.text: Then I said to them, “The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
Ezekiel then said to them, “The LORD’s word came to me, saying,” The prophet answers by reporting a word that came to him, not by offering his own first account of the death. The explanation will be the LORD’s. The people’s question is met with a messenger’s heading.

Arminian readers hear the prophet pointing them to the LORD’s word, a meaning that will come from the same voice that commanded the unmourned morning, and a word they can hear as addressed to them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same reply as Ezekiel’s faithful turn to the word that came to him, the only explanation he offers for the act they have seen.

Shared ground: the meaning is the LORD’s word. The heading is simple, and the speech follows.

verses.text: ‘Speak to the house of Israel, “The Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and that which your soul pities; and your sons and your daughters whom you have left behind will fall by the sword.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says, “Behold, I will profane my sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and that which your soul pities; and your sons and your daughters whom you have left behind will fall by the sword.” The sanctuary is his, and he will profane it. It is their pride, the desire of their eyes, and that which their soul pities—the same tender phrase now used of the house they loved. Sons and daughters left behind will fall by the sword. The two losses are set side by side, the holy place and the children, and both are told with restraint.

Arminian readers hear a word that interprets the prophet’s marriage-loss as the coming loss of the sanctuary, and a warning about sons and daughters still in the city, a grief the exiles are asked to face as their own.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same profaning of the sanctuary, named as the pride of their power and the desire of their eyes, and the fall of the sons and daughters left behind, as the Lord GOD’s own explanation of the sign.

Shared ground: the desire of their eyes is the sanctuary, and the children left behind are in danger of the sword. The two loves are named together.

verses.text: You will do as I have done. You won’t cover your lips or eat mourner’s bread.
verses.arminianNotes:
“You will do as I have done. You won’t cover your lips or eat mourner’s bread.” The people will copy the prophet’s sign. The covered lips and the mourner’s bread, refused to him, will be refused to them. The coming loss will be too large, or too stunning, for the usual rites, as his was.

Arminian readers hear a people who will find themselves doing what they now watch, a future they can still understand as the meaning of this morning’s strange obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same “You will do as I have done.” with uncovered lips and no mourner’s bread, as the Lord GOD’s word about how they will bear the coming blow.

Shared ground: they will do as the prophet has done. The withheld rites are the shared sign.

verses.text: Your turbans will be on your heads, and your sandals on your feet. You won’t mourn or weep; but you will pine away in your iniquities, and moan one toward another.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Your turbans will be on your heads, and your sandals on your feet. You won’t mourn or weep; but you will pine away in your iniquities, and moan one toward another.” Head-coverings stay on; sandals stay on. They will not mourn or weep in the ordinary way, and yet they will pine away in their iniquities and moan to one another. The grief is not denied; it is turned inward, a moaning between neighbors, in the guilt the verse names as theirs.

Arminian readers hear a people who will still suffer, pining and moaning, even when the public forms of mourning are gone, a sorrow bound up with iniquities they cannot disown.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the turbans and sandals, the absence of ordinary mourning and weeping, and the pining away in iniquities with moaning toward one another, as the Lord GOD’s account of their coming state.

Shared ground: they will not mourn in the usual way, and they will pine and moan. The iniquities are named as the soil of that wasting.

verses.text: Thus Ezekiel will be a sign to you; according to all that he has done, you will do. When this comes, then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.’ ” ’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Thus Ezekiel will be a sign to you; according to all that he has done, you will do. When this comes, then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.” The prophet, named in the third person inside the LORD’s speech, is himself the sign. What he has done, they will do; and when it comes, they will know that he is the Lord GOD. The knowledge of the LORD is the end of the sign, as so often in this book.

Arminian readers hear a sign meant to be recognized when the blow falls, a knowledge of the Lord GOD offered through the prophet’s acted word, which the people will then be able to read.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same naming of Ezekiel as a sign, the matching of their future acts to his, and the knowledge of the Lord GOD when it comes, as the purpose the LORD himself states.

Shared ground: Ezekiel is a sign, and they will know that he is the Lord GOD. The traditions share that purpose.

verses.text: “You, son of man, shouldn’t it be in the day when I take from them their strength, the joy of their glory, the desire of their eyes, and that whereupon they set their heart—their sons and their daughters—
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD turns again to the prophet: in the day when he takes from them their strength, the joy of their glory, the desire of their eyes, and that whereupon they set their heart—their sons and their daughters—the thought is left running into the next verse. The same loves are listed again: strength, glory, the desire of their eyes, the heart’s treasure, and the children. The day is the day of that taking.

Arminian readers hear a list that gathers all they have set their heart on, including their sons and daughters, a coming day the exiles can already begin to understand in the light of the prophet’s own loss.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same day and the same list—their strength, the joy of their glory, the desire of their eyes, and their sons and daughters—as the LORD’s description of what he will take from them.

Shared ground: the desire of their eyes and their children stand together in the list. The sentence is completed in the arrival of the one who escapes.

verses.text: that in that day he who escapes will come to you, to cause you to hear it with your ears?
verses.arminianNotes:
“that in that day he who escapes will come to you, to cause you to hear it with your ears?” The escapee will come to Ezekiel and cause him to hear it. The news of the city’s fall will arrive in a survivor’s mouth. The line is still the LORD’s, and it announces that coming as a sure part of the day already named. Classical Arminians take that announced coming as a future God truly knows and will bring to pass, not as an open outcome he merely waits to observe.

Arminian readers hear a real traveler who will reach the prophet, a hearing with the ears, a word of fulfillment that will not be rumor only.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same escapee, coming in that day to cause the prophet to hear it with his ears, as the LORD’s appointed means of bringing the news.

Shared ground: someone will escape, and will come, and the prophet will hear it. The question form still belongs to a word that expects this to take place.

verses.text: In that day your mouth will be opened to him who has escaped, and you will speak and be no more mute. So you will be a sign to them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“In that day your mouth will be opened to him who has escaped, and you will speak and be no more mute. So you will be a sign to them. Then they will know that I am the LORD.” When the survivor comes, the prophet’s mouth will be opened, and he will be no more mute, and will be a sign, and they will know that he is the LORD. This opening of the mouth looks back to the muteness announced in 3:26–27, and 33:21–22 later reports it when a survivor brings news that the city has been defeated. The verse itself promises that he will speak again, and that the opened mouth will be a sign.

Arminian readers hear a mouth opened for a real word to the one who has escaped, a muteness that will end, and a knowledge of the LORD that the people can then receive.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the same opening of the mouth, the end of muteness, the prophet as a sign, and the knowledge that he is the LORD, as the LORD’s own close to the sign-act.

Shared ground: the mouth will be opened, and they will know that he is the LORD. The day of the escapee is the day the sign is complete.
